commentary.seminaVerbi:
Malachi’s refiner reads like alchemical calcination: the same heat that destroys dross reveals essence, a ruthless mercy. Jung’s individuation gives it a psychological grammar: the Self arrives as an intolerable purity, and the ego discovers it cannot “stand” without being remade.

Simeon’s long waiting resembles the Hindu jivanmukta at the edge of release, or the Buddhist arhat nearing parinirvana: peace is not escape but completion, the moment the vow dissolves because the sight has happened. The child as “light” parallels the Buddhist imagery of prajna dispelling avidya; speculation: the temple scene stages awakening as recognition rather than acquisition.

“A sign contradicted” matches the Tao Te Ching’s soft power that provokes the hard, and Socrates’ gadfly whose very presence exposes. Mary’s pierced soul echoes the bodhisattva’s compassion that includes suffering as the cost of seeing others’ hearts without illusion.
commentary.excursus:
Malachi promises a “messenger” who makes the way, then warns that what follows is not comfort but chemistry: fire, lye, scrubbing until the thing confesses what it is. The desire for God is exposed as a desire for clean surfaces, for a world where the stain can be named and burned out. But the dread is that the refiner doesn’t punish; he purifies. He keeps going until even the priests are reduced to metal.

Luke stages that purification as domestic obedience. Mary and Joseph do everything right, pay the small, poor price, and the Temple receives them like any other couple. Yet the old man waiting for “consolation” is the first to admit the trap: to see salvation is to be dismissed, to be allowed to die. Simeon’s peace is not relief; it’s closure. He clutches the child like a verdict.

The child is called “light,” but the light is interrogation. “A sign contradicted” means the world will organize itself against him because he makes hidden motives visible. The sword promised to Mary is not only grief; it is insight forced into her, the maternal bond turned into a wound that opens thought. Anna’s fasting is the body rehearsing that same logic: desire narrowed to a point so sharp it can speak. The Temple is not a cradle but a furnace, and everyone in it is already being refined.
commentary.synthesis: God’s visitation purifies before it pacifies: the Messiah enters the temple under the Law and becomes the decisive sign that judges hearts while extending salvation beyond Israel to the nations.

gospel.text: Luke binds promise to legality and to pneumatology: written law marks the child as “holy,” while the Spirit privately certifies Simeon, fusing objective ordinance and subjective recognition without letting either stand alone.

The episode is a hinge between temple and home. Prophecy erupts in the cultic center, then the narrative deliberately returns to Nazareth and ordinary growth—suggesting the redemption announced in the temple will be carried forward through hidden years before public manifestation.

reading.text: Malachi frames the divine advent as covenant litigation: a messenger inaugurates a courtroom, and the question is not whether God will come but whether anyone can remain intact under his arrival.
The target is the sacrificial system’s credibility. Purified priests generate “justice” in worship, so restored cult becomes a social-theological reset, not a private spirituality.

marginalia.text: “Send my angel”: God precedes himself; arrival is staged, not improvised.
“The Lord… the angel of the testament”: titles pile up; identity comes as a riddle.
Coming is not comfort but endurance-test: “who shall stand”.
Fire and lye: purification by violence; holiness has a caustic smell.
He “shall sit”: judgment is patient, deliberate, not a flare of temper.
Priests first: cult must be purified at the source before it can speak for the people.
“As in the days of old”: renewal is described as recovery, not innovation.
Purification after birth: the Holy enters under a regimen made for the unclean.
Two birds: poverty becomes the offering that carries the Offering.
“Waiting”: Israel reduced to a verb; hope as a vocation.
Temple meeting: law’s choreography becomes the stage for recognition.
Dismissal language: the faithful die by permission, not by accident.
“Before the face”: salvation is public, not esoteric.
Light for Gentiles, glory for Israel: universality without erasing election.
Set “for fall… resurrection”: the same stone does both; neutrality is excluded.
“Sign contradicted”: truth arrives as contention, not consensus.
Mary’s interior is not spared; proximity to the Christ is wounding.
Night-and-day worship: time itself is tithed.

lines: Behold I send my angel, and he shall prepare the way before my face. And presently the Lord, whom you seek, and the angel of the testament, whom you desire, shall come to his temple. Behold, he cometh, saith the Lord of hosts. My angel... Viz., John the Baptist, the messenger of God, and forerunner of Christ.
And who shall be able to think of the day of his coming? and who shall stand to see him? for he is like a refining fire, and like the fuller's herb:
And he shall sit refining and cleansing the silver, and he shall purify the sons of Levi, and shall refine them as gold, and as silver, and they shall offer sacrifices to the Lord in justice.
And the sacrifice of Juda and of Jerusalem shall please the Lord, as in the days of old, and in the ancient years.
readings.heading: A reading from the Book of Malachi

lines: And after the days of her purification, according to the law of Moses, were accomplished, they carried him to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord:
As it is written in the law of the Lord: Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord:
And to offer a sacrifice, according as it is written in the law of the Lord, a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons:
And behold there was a man in Jerusalem named Simeon: and this man was just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel. And the Holy Ghost was in him.
And he had received an answer from the Holy Ghost, that he should not see death before he had seen the Christ of the Lord.
And he came by the Spirit into the temple. And when his parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the law,
He also took him into his arms and blessed God and said
Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace:
Because my eyes have seen thy salvation,
Which thou hast prepared before the face of all peoples:
A light to the revelation of the Gentiles and the glory of thy people Israel.
And his father and mother were wondering at those things which were spoken concerning him.

And Simeon blessed them and said to Mary his mother: Behold this child is set for the fall and for the resurrection of many in Israel and for a sign which shall be contradicted. For the fall, etc... Christ came for the salvation of all men; but here Simeon prophesies what would come to pass, that many through their own wilful blindness and obstinacy would not believe in Christ, nor receive his doctrine, which therefore would be ruin to them: but to others a resurrection, by their believing in him, and obeying his commandments.
And thy own soul a sword shall pierce, that, out of many hearts thoughts may be revealed.
And there was one Anna, a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Aser. She was far advanced in years and had lived with her husband seven years from her virginity.
And she was a widow until fourscore and four years: who departed not from the temple, by fastings and prayers serving night and day.
Now she, at the same hour, coming in, confessed to the Lord: and spoke of him to all that looked for the redemption of Israel.
And after they had performed all things according to the law of the Lord, they returned into Galilee, to their city Nazareth.
And the child grew and waxed strong, full of wisdom: and the grace of God was in him.
